Fisheye depth · label-free adaptation · 2026-09-08

Depth at the Rim

Depth models are bad at the edge of a fisheye image. On a head-worn camera, the edge is where your hands are. Here is why it happens, and how far it can be fixed without depth labels.

DA3-Small · DA3-Large · VGGT · VGGT-Omega Aria Digital Twin · 2 rooms · 2 devices Every bar written down before the run
Part 1

Motivation

A fisheye lens packs more of the world into each ring of pixels as you move outward. Objects near the edge get fewer pixels. They also come out radially squashed.

Depth models are trained on ordinary photos. They have never seen this.

And the edge is where a wearable needs to work. The centre of the frame is the far wall. Your hands, your body, the desk — all at the edge.

How much worse is the edge?

We split each image by incidence angle — how far a pixel sits from the lens axis — and by true distance. Two zones matter:

  • Rim — beyond 38°, closer than 2 m. Hands, body, desk.
  • Centre — within 11°. Mostly the far wall.

Error is relative: how far off the depth is, as a fraction of the truth. Each frame is first aligned to ground truth by scale and offset, so global scale earns nothing. Only the shape counts.

Four off-the-shelf depth models, same 20 frames. Error is the typical fractional mistake: 0.389 means the predicted depth is off by about 39%. Lower is better. The two error columns are not directly comparable between models (VGGT-Omega runs at a different internal resolution) — the ratio in the last column is.
Depth modelError at the rimError at the centreRim ÷ centre
DA3-Small0.3890.1832.13
DA3-Large0.1910.0942.04
VGGT0.2040.0792.57
VGGT-Omega0.1470.0632.33

The rim is about twice as bad as the centre, in every model.

These four differ by 2.4× in raw accuracy and the ratio barely moves, so a bigger model does not fix it. The four figures above are each from one recording; across thirteen the ratio averages 2.2 and ranges from about 1.4 to 2.7 — see the note at the end of this section.

Part 2

Data

Everything runs on Aria Digital Twin — Meta camera-glasses recordings with dense depth on every frame. Two things about it matter.

Two rooms, not one. Six sequences in an apartment, two in a small office. The office used a different pair of glasses, with a different lens. That second room is our only honest test, and most conclusions below turn on it.

One apartment sequence is the same room with the furniture moved. A method can score well on the other test recording just by memorising the room. This one catches that.

One detail that cost us a whole result

Room 2's lens differs by half a percent in focal length and nearly two degrees in field of view. Score it with the wrong lens and you get a smooth error growing toward the edge — which looks exactly like "bad at the rim". Every sequence is scored with its own calibration.

Part 3

Method

Take a strong depth model. Freeze it. Attach a small adapter — about 123,000 trainable parameters against a model of hundreds of millions. Nothing here retrains a foundation model.

Three rules make the results mean something.

  1. Every claim gets a twin. Each idea runs against a control identical but for the one thing tested. If the control improves too, the idea was not the cause. Five earlier methods here died to their own controls.
  2. The bar is set before the run. Success and refutation both go into git before anything executes. Several results below are failures against our own bars.
  3. The real test is a different room. More footage from the room a method was built in flatters it.
  4. One recording is not a test set. We learned this late — see the correction in §4.4. Numbers should be a mean over many recordings with a spread, and where one is still a single recording, we say so.
A trap worth knowing

Because every frame is scale-and-offset aligned before scoring, a method that only rescales depth globally scores zero by construction. That is deliberate. Only a change in the shape of the depth map can win.

Part 4

Results

Eight findings, in the order we found them. Each one made the next possible.

How to read the numbers below

Almost every percentage from here on is a change in depth error against some baseline, so negative is better and positive is worse. −26% means the error dropped by about a quarter; +22% means it grew by about a fifth. Table headers say which baseline each one is measured against. Where a table compares options, green marks the better outcome and red the worse — even when both are positive.

Four recordings are used for testing throughout, and they always carry the same names: Same room and Same room, rearranged are the apartment; New room A and New room B are the two recordings from the small office — "room 2" in the text — filmed on a different pair of glasses.

4.1  Tilting the camera hurts — for the wrong reason

A head-worn camera rolls with the head. So how much tilt matters?

We rotated the virtual camera and re-rendered. We did not rotate the picture — rotating a picture adds black corners, and that turns out to be a separate problem entirely.

The inputs — the camera is rotated, then the scene re-rendered

Where the error goes — brighter is worse

How much the whole-image error grows when the camera is tilted, measured against that same model with the camera level. Positive is worse: +46% means the error is nearly half again as large.
Depth modelPretrained onTilted ±20°±30°±40°
DA3-Smallsingle photos+13%+46%+131%*
DA3-Largesingle photos+10%+52%+114%
VGGTmulti-view geometry+7%+11%+23%
VGGT-Omegamulti-view geometry+3%+11%+11%

Tilt sensitivity comes from the pretraining data, not from depth estimation.

Multi-view-pretrained models see cameras at every orientation by construction. They are 4–5× less sensitive at 30° and more accurate. Size does not help: DA3-Large is twice as accurate as DA3-Small when level, and slightly worse when tilted.

Then we measured real head tilt. The glasses record their own orientation and gravity, so this is read off the data. Across 60,105 frames: median 3.7°, 99th percentile 21.8°, nothing past 40°.

The model is flat to about ±20°. The data almost never leaves ±20°. Measured independently, they line up: 98.5% of real frames sit in the model's comfortable range.

But those are two numbers put side by side, not an answer. The answer is what you get when you multiply them — how much depth error does real head roll actually cost? Nobody had worked that out, because the tilt curve had only ever been measured at 20°, 30° and 40°, and nine tenths of real head roll is under 15°. So we measured it there.

So ignoring roll costs about one and a half percent. That is cheap enough to ignore — and it is now a measurement rather than two numbers that happened to line up.

Two things in that picture are worth more than the headline, though.

The rare frames carry a quarter of the cost. Tilts beyond ±20° are 1.5% of all frames and account for 26% of the total — an eighteen-fold concentration, because the curve climbs so steeply out there. So "ignore roll" and "handle rare big tilts" are both right, and they are different products: a correction applied to every frame, versus a detector that flags the occasional one.

One thing was still missing, though. Both figures above are for the most roll-sensitive of our four models — and §4.3 recommends a different one. So we measured all four the same way.

So the advice sharpens twice. If you use a multi-view-pretrained model — which §4.3 recommends anyway — roll costs half a percent and there is nothing to do about it. The "handle the rare tilt" advice applies to the single-photo models and not to those.

And a familiar shape returns: DA3-Large costs 1.85%, the same as DA3-Small's 1.80% — despite being far better at 30°. Almost all real roll is under 15°, where the two are alike. Making the single-photo model bigger does nothing for the cost you actually pay; changing what it was pretrained on divides it by four. That is the same lesson as §4.1: for this family of problems, scale is not the axis that helps.

Tilting one way is twice as bad as the other — for one of the four models. At 30°, tilting one direction costs 24% and the other 56%, and every earlier version of this report averaged the two into a single "±30° = +46%". The asymmetry only appears past about 20°, and it was invisible until we measured the two signs separately.

…and then we checked whether it was really about the models

Three things in our pipeline are not left-right symmetric — we rotate every image a quarter turn before the model sees it, the lens centre sits a few pixels off the middle, and the wearer's hands are always low and to one side. Any of those could produce this signature with no help from the model. So we ran the same test on four different depth models, which all see exactly the same pixels.

It came out undecided, and the honest answer is "partly both". All four models lean the same way, which is what a rendering quirk would do. But the size differs six-fold between models that see identical images, and the second DA3 model shows no consistent lean at all (4 times out of 8, a coin flip), which a rendering quirk would not do.

So the 24%-versus-56% figure above is a result about DA3-Small, the model with the largest and noisiest asymmetry of the four. It reproduces on that model (7 of 8 recordings here, 11 of 13 earlier). It should not be quoted as a fact about depth models in general, and we cannot yet say how much of it is our own rendering.

One last check on this section, because a later part of this report (§4.4) found that the single recording we used for a while was a bad one. So we re-measured both of the numbers above across thirteen recordings.

Nothing here changes a conclusion. The rim is about twice as bad as the centre on every recording we tried, the cost of tilting still climbs steeply (+12% → +40% → +92%), and the comparison between model families was always a ratio measured on the same frames, so shifting the baseline leaves it alone.

It does add one honest caveat to the part that matters most. ±20° is cheap on average — +12% — but not on every recording: the spread reaches +21%. "Almost free" is a mean, not a guarantee.

4.2  A hard black border is worse than tilting

This was an accident. Rotating a fisheye picture adds black wedges. We wanted to know what the wedges alone cost.

A black border of the given width is painted around an otherwise clean view, and the depth is scored on a region 14° inside it. The picture itself is unchanged; only what sits outside that region differs.
Width of the black borderShare of the frame it coversDepth error grows by
5 px3.1%+22%
12 px7.5%+13%
25 px15.2%+17%
45 px26.5%+17%
70 px39.5%+6.6%
100 px53.4%+32%

A border hurts by how close it is, not by how big it is.

Blacking out 3% of the frame costs about as much as blacking out 40%. Move the scored region right up against the border instead of 14° away, and the error grows by +106% instead.

Tolerance is model-specific, on a completely different axis from tilt:

The most transferable warning here

DA3-Large is the most accurate of the four on a clean frame and the one that breaks hardest with a border — a 4.6× collapse from a change that touches no scored pixel. Pick on clean-benchmark accuracy and you would choose it, then lose most of that accuracy to a letterbox, a crop pad, a lens hood, or a mask.

The numbers in the table above are from one recording. Across thirteen the costs are +59% ± 14 and +269% ± 62, and the collapse is 4.6× rather than the 7.4× we first reported — see below. The "worst of the four" half was measured on all four models once; we have since re-measured two of them, so treat it as established for the DA3 pair and untested for the others.

Both of the numbers in this section came from one recording, and §4.4 explains why that turned out to matter. So we re-measured the whole of §4.2 across thirteen.

This is the outcome we would have hoped for from a check like this: the advice came out stronger and the numbers came out smaller. "Never put a hard border next to what you care about" and "cost is proximity, not area" now rest on thirteen recordings instead of one. A 4.6× collapse is still the most useful warning in this report.

4.3  Teaching the model with no labels

The same frozen model is far more accurate when shown the scene as an ordinary photo instead of a fisheye. It knows what is out there. It just cannot read it through the fisheye.

So: take its answer from the rectified view, map it back into fisheye coordinates, and train the adapter to copy it. No depth labels anywhere.

The first version failed. To cover the whole fisheye cone, the rectified view must be so wide that a fifth of it is black — and per 4.2, that wrecked the teacher. A narrower view kept the teacher accurate but reached only 70% of the rim. Accuracy and coverage were in conflict.

Finding 4.2 broke the conflict. VGGT-Omega tolerates a border, so it can run the wide view at full coverage and stay accurate.

Before training anything: is the teacher actually better than the raw model at the rim? Scored only on pixels the teacher can see. The first two rows use an identical view with an identical black frame, so they differ only in which model is the teacher. The last column is the average over thirteen recordings; the ordering it shows held on all thirteen.

Same checkpoints, second room, other glasses. Nothing retrained.

The control transfers nothing. In the original room it carried most of the gain. In a new room it is worth zero. It learned "imitate a stronger model on these pictures", and that does not travel.

Every label-free method beats real labels once the room changes. Labelled training fits one room and cannot take it anywhere.

So what is transferable? We swapped the adapter for something that can express one thing only: a correction curve depending on incidence angle. Sixteen numbers, fitted on the apartment, applied unchanged everywhere.

In a new room, sixteen numbers match the adapter or beat it. The transferable part is a recalibration of depth against viewing angle. We first assumed that made it a property of the lens. §4.6 shows it is not. At home the adapter is far ahead of the curve — by more than this table says; see the correction immediately below.

A correction to the "same room" row above

That row is marked with a star because we no longer trust it. Every in-room number in this report was measured on one recording, chosen once at the start and used ever since. Thirteen more recordings from the same room and the same glasses had been sitting unused, so we finally scored the same unchanged curve on all of them.

The sting is in the amber square. "Same room, rearranged" — the recording we have been calling the harder test all along — is the representative one, a third of a standard deviation from the middle. The number that read like a pessimistic sanity check was the honest one. The number that read like the result was the fluke.

Two things are unaffected. The effect is real: all thirteen improve, and the two-number control makes things worse on all thirteen. And the cross-room numbers in the table were measured on different recordings entirely, so they are not touched by this.

We then re-measured the adapter the same way. It was inflated too — but only about half as much, so the gap between them widens:

What the correction actually did to the conclusions

Two headline numbers came down. Everything they supported held or improved. The adapter beats the curve by more than we said — 5.5× at home, not 3.1×, because the curve was flattered about twice as hard. And the comparison §4.3 rests on — the rectified teacher beating the plain one — now holds on 13 recordings out of 13 instead of on one.

We have since re-run the label-trained model as well, so every same-room number in this report is now an average over thirteen recordings. All four came down; every ratio between them went up. The reason is visible in the table: the weakest method, the 16-number curve, was flattered about twice as hard (×2.4) as the three trained ones (×1.3 to ×1.4).

That last point is worth keeping. A 16-number fit is far more sensitive to which recording you score it on than a trained adapter is — its spread is 24% of its effect against the adapter's 13%. Claims about the curve need more recordings than claims about the adapter.

The thing we would tell anyone starting this

Our three training seeds differ by 2.9 points. The recordings differ by about 5. We spent the whole project measuring the smaller of the two.

Two footnotes. The curve is smooth enough for a quadratic, so in practice it is six numbers. And it changes from one depth model to another — a calibration procedure, not a table anyone publishes once.

A separate line of this project fits the same curve from camera motion instead — no teacher involved. Same shape, same size (−15.4% against −16.6% on one sequence). Two unrelated label-free signals, estimating the same object.

How much footage does the fit need? We predicted "a lot, from many viewpoints": the curve is pinned down by how widely depth varies inside each angle band, and one camera position sees a narrow slice. We wrote that down, then tested it.

About 30 frames is enough — if someone is walking while they are recorded.

Varied viewpoints buy nothing over a single recording at matched frame count. Two frames is too few: the answer swings 13 points between draws. By thirty it is within a couple of points of the full-data fit. The catch is in 4.5 — the frames have to contain motion.

4.5  What the fit needs is walking, not the right lens

Should you fit the curve on the camera it will run on? It is the same lens, so it ought to win. We tested it on room 2's own footage — teacher-supervised, no ground truth anywhere in the fit.

It lost, badly.

The frames being scored are identical across these rows. The only thing that changes is which footage the curve was fitted on beforehand.
Curve fitted onCameraWearerNew room ANew room B
Apartment, 240 frameswrongwalking around−26.0%−8.9%
New room B, 60 framesrightbarely moving−2.6%—
New room A, 60 framesrightbarely moving—−3.8%

The wrong lens with motion beats the right lens without it — by about 10×.

So the fit does not really need your camera. It needs frames where the camera moved.

We can say why, because it was measured. Refit on random 30-frame subsets and see how far the answer moves between draws: 0.060 for walking footage, 0.127 for near-static. Static frames are worth about half as much each.

That left one thing unsettled. Room 2 is our only second camera and our only near-static footage, so "the target camera is the problem" and "the footage is static" were tangled together. We could separate them without new data, by staying inside the apartment.

First we measured the motion, which we had been asserting rather than checking. The camera's own position is recorded, so this is read off the data: the apartment wearer walks about 40 m per clip; the room-2 wearer moves 2.4 m in total.

Then the control. From the same apartment footage we picked two sets of 30 frames — one where the camera roamed, one where it barely left a spot — and fitted the curve on each. Same camera, same room, same everything except how far the wearer walked.

So the honest limit is now closed, and the advice sharpens. The fitting frames should span roughly 2 metres of walking. That is something a person can actually do; "frames with motion in them" was not.

A trap we nearly fell into

Averaged over five repeats, the low-motion curve looks perfectly reasonable — a smooth arch, much like the good one. The instability only shows up when you compare the repeats against each other. A single fit that looks fine can be worthless, so check that it predicts angles it was not fitted on.

4.6  It is not really about the lens

We had been calling this curve a property of the lens. That was an assumption, not a measurement — every comparison so far changed the camera and the room, the scene and the wearer at the same time.

So we changed only the lens. The same footage can be re-rendered through a different lens shape covering exactly the same cone: same rays, same content, nothing missing, only the spacing of the pixels across the angle changes. We did that for four lens shapes, fitted a curve on each, and then applied each curve to each lens — sixteen combinations.

Using a lens's own curve rather than another lens's is worth about one percentage point — less than the noise between repeats. Matching the lens buys nothing.

What does matter is which lens shape you fit on. So we widened the test to six shapes, from one that squeezes the outer part of the picture hardest to one that stretches it hardest, and fitted a curve on each.

So there is a single best thing to fit on, and it is not your own lens. The squeezing shapes beat the real lens's own curve on every one of thirteen recordings, by 4.0 points on average. The differences between the squeezing shapes themselves are inside the noise, so the useful advice is the direction, not a particular shape.

"Matching does not help" holds across the four shapes that look like real fisheye lenses. It stops holding for the two extremes, which are far enough from a fisheye that only their own curve fits them. That boundary is worth knowing before anyone applies this to an unusual camera.

We thought we knew why. Stretching the outer part of a picture creates extra pixels by interpolation — more of them, carrying no new information. So we tested it. The camera files are natively 1408 pixels across and everything above had been reading them at 504, which means the stretching really was inventing detail that existed in the file.

Reading the source at double the resolution — the same experiment in every other respect — should then have pulled the shapes together.

Two explanations tried, two dead

We first said squeezing wins because it gives the rim more pixels. That was backwards. We then said stretching loses because its extra pixels are invented. That is now refuted too.

What is left has to be about where the content sits across the picture — the same rays, the same sharpness, arranged differently from the centre outwards. That echoes §4.2, where what mattered was position in the frame and not how much of it was affected. We are not offering a third guess.

The advice is unaffected either way, and now has a second leg to stand on: the ordering repeats at both source resolutions with the same slope, so it is not a quirk of how we read the files.

One more thing had to be checked before recommending any of this. Everything above used the same depth model. Does the ordering belong to the problem, or just to that model? We repeated it on DA3-Large — the one that collapses by 636% when you put a border next to it, so about as different in its reaction to the edge of a frame as anything we have.

So the rule about which shape to use travels. How much you gain does not. On the easy recording DA3-Large gets less than half of what DA3-Small got; on the hard one the best shape manages −0.7% and every other one makes things worse.

A plain arithmetic reading, offered as that and nothing more: DA3-Large already has half the rim error to start with (0.191 against 0.389 in §4.1's table). A correction that removes a systematic mistake can only do so much when there is less of it.

Re-render your footage to squeeze the outer edge, fit the curve there, then use it on your real images.

Worth 4.0 ± 1.3 points on the real lens, measured across thirteen recordings, and positive on every one of them. It costs one resample. This is the first thing in this report that makes a result better rather than just warning you off something — but see the end of this section for how far the gain travels.

What we changed our minds about

Earlier sections called the curve "a property of the lens". That is wrong, and it is wrong in the one way that matters: it names the lens, and the lens is the thing nobody had varied. The accurate version is a property of how the model's error grows with viewing angle — largely independent of how a lens spreads pixels across that angle. It also makes calibration a genuine one-off rather than a per-camera step.

One limit: these are four re-renderings of the same footage, so they share optics, sharpness and sensor. This establishes independence from the geometry, which is what the curve is indexed by — not from everything the word "lens" covers.

4.7  Three things that did not work

Each failed against a bar we had written down first. Each rules something out.

  • Wider teacher coverage. We pushed rim coverage from 70% to 99% using stretched views. Coverage rose; the teacher's accuracy there fell 9.5%, and the student got worse. A student follows the teacher's accuracy, not its coverage. No label beats a bad label.
  • Telling the network about the lens. We fed in the lens's local distortion per pixel, then tested on two unseen lenses. It lost to randomly shuffled values, and to feeding nothing. But it beat the wrong lens's values 16 times out of 16. So the network does read the input — real geometry is simply no better than an arbitrary fixed pattern, while contradictory geometry hurts.
  • Depth from camera motion. Triangulating across three frames gives metric anchors at about 4% error, where the model is at 44%. It beat both controls on all six sequences. But the locked bar asked the correction to fix the distortion, not just the numbers, and it failed that on all six. A recalibration, not a solution.

4.8  More data from the same room buys nothing

The obvious objection is that our training sets are small. We tested it: computation held fixed, only the number of distinct frames changing.

Every row does the same amount of training; only the number of different frames it was shown changes. The last column is the error in the middle of the image, which the adapter is not supposed to touch.
Different frames seenSame roomSame room, rearrangedError at the centre
240−67.1%−21.7%+58%
2,400−69.3%−18.9%+101%
4,800−69.9%−21.0%+128%
11,418−71.3%−20.9%+145%

48× more frames moved the honest test by nothing, and made the centre 2.5× worse.

The bottleneck is not how much footage you have. It is how many different places it comes from.

Part 5

Conclusion

What to do

  • Never put a hard black border next to what you care about. No crops, no masks, no zero padding. To rotate, rotate the camera and re-render. Cost is set by proximity, not area — and with the wrong model it is catastrophic.
  • Do not spend effort on camera tilt. Ignoring it costs 0.3–0.5% of depth error with a multi-view-pretrained model and about 1.8% with a single-photo one, integrated over how often people actually tilt their heads. If you are on a single-photo model and still care, the only thing worth handling is the rare tilt past ±20°, which is 1.5% of frames and a quarter of the cost.
  • Pick the depth model for robustness, not clean-benchmark accuracy. They do not correlate. Our most accurate model fell apart at the first framing artefact.
  • You can adapt to a fisheye with no depth labels. Distil a stronger frozen model through a rectified view. Expect about 94% of what real labels buy in the room you trained in — measured across thirteen recordings, and higher than the 89% we first published from one.
  • Expect almost none of it to transfer. What crosses a room is a small angle-dependent recalibration — six numbers — and that beats labelled training in a new room. About 30 frames fit it, and they should span roughly 2 m of walking. Footage from the right camera does not make up for a camera that stayed still — and it does not need to be the right camera at all (§4.6).
  • Re-render to squeeze the outer edge before you fit. Fit the curve on a version of your footage that gives the outer part of the view less of the frame, then apply it to the real images. Worth 4.0 ± 1.3 points and positive on all thirteen recordings we tried. Any of several shapes work; the direction is what matters. Check what it is worth on your own model before shipping it — the ordering holds on a stronger model but most of the gain does not, and the most stretched shape turns actively harmful.
  • Do not fix generalisation with more footage from the same room. 48× more bought nothing and made another region worse.

What we are not claiming

  • Most results are one seed. The label-free result has three. The others rest on consistent direction (16 of 16, 6 of 6) and on bars set in advance — not on any single large difference.
  • Every same-room number in this report was originally measured on a single recording that turned out to be an outlier, and all of them have since been re-measured across thirteen. The exception is the "rearranged room" column, still a single recording — though we now know it is a representative one.
  • That recording has a pattern worth naming, because it will apply to anyone repeating this work: it exaggerated everything we did to the images and nothing we merely measured about them. Nine separate interventions came out 0.5 to 6.0 standard deviations stronger on it than the average — including ones that made things worse, which came out worse still — while three plain measurements read normal. So the rim penalty and the tilt curve were fine as published; every method's effect, helpful or harmful, was overstated.
  • The "82%" companion to §4.3's headline is still that single recording, unlike the 94% beside it, which is thirteen.
  • The cross-room test is 120 frames over two sequences where the wearer moved 2.4 m in total. It carries several claims above and is the weakest link. §4.5 replaces the worst of that dependence with a control inside the apartment, but room 2 is still small.
  • The tilt data is people doing household tasks, standing and walking. It says nothing about lying down, working under a car, or cycling — exactly where the assumption breaks.
  • §4.6's four lenses are re-renderings of one recording, so they share optics, sharpness and sensor. It shows the curve does not depend on lens geometry; it does not show it survives a genuinely different piece of glass.
  • In the tilt experiment we could not fully separate "changed the projection" from "removed the black border". A fisheye circle does not fit its square frame, so any rotation disturbs the boundary. That stays open.

What we would do next

  • Make room 2 a real test set instead of 120 frames. This is now clearly the biggest weakness left. Every same-room figure is an average over thirteen recordings; every cross-room figure is still two, both nearly static. More apartment footage cannot fix that — it needs a second room recorded properly.
  • Work out why squeezing helps. Two explanations are dead and we stopped looking. The obvious next probe — shrinking the picture into a smaller circle to move content inward — introduces a border, and §4.2 says that is fatal. A third attempt, mirroring the input, was void because we mirrored the image and not the ground truth. Someone needs a design that avoids both traps; we did not find one worth the runs.
  • Combine the two label-free signals — the rectified teacher and the motion-triangulated anchors. They estimate the same thing, and each needs something the other does not.
Where the detail lives

Every number comes from a committed run artefact, and every protocol was written before its run. The full technical record — per-experiment controls, and the corrections we had to make to our own earlier readings — sits alongside this in the project repository.
